source.title: Large Language Models Are Involuntary Truth-Tellers: Exploiting Fallacy Failure for Jailbreak Attacks
source.authors: Yue Zhou; Henry Peng Zou; Barbara Maria Di Eugenio; Yang Zhang

record.tranche_reason: The study reports harmful-response rates for GCG, an adversarial suffix attack, on its own evaluated models. This is a different method and setting from the original first-token work, but it measures whether a suffix-based attack can bypass refusal.
record.gate_note: The study also evaluates FFA, other jailbreak baselines, and defenses. FFA is a fallacious-reasoning prompt attack, not a test of the listed opening-token mechanisms; its primary attack results are recorded as findings outside the claim versions. GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Gemini baseline values marked with daggers are identified as results from previous papers and are not recorded as this study's results. The paper does not measure fine-tuning, per-token KL, parameter localization, or deepening safety training.
record.test_reason: The study runs GCG, an adversarial-suffix attack, itself on Vicuna-7b and LLaMA-3-8B and reports bypass and harmfulness rates against a naive baseline. This bears on V4's claim that suffixes defeat refusal. GCG is only a baseline next to the paper's own FFA attack, so this is a weak, incidental test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that none of the three defenses (perplexity filter, paraphrasing, retokenization) effectively stops FFA. They frame models' inability to produce deliberate fallacies as a security threat with implications for self-verification and hallucination.
record.recipe_differences: This study evaluates jailbreak prompts, including GCG adversarial token sequences, rather than measuring aligned-versus-base per-token KL or testing compliant response prefills.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model: FFA is substantially less effective on LLaMA-3 than on GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and Vicuna-7b. The paper also reports that paraphrasing and retokenization change FFA performance, but these are not tests of the claim's first-token mechanism.

fits_no_version.finding: FFA, which asks for a fallacious but deceptively real procedure, gave high bypass and harm scores on GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Gemini-Pro and Vicuna-7b, and weaker scores on LLaMA-3-8B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A fallacious-reasoning prompt attack elicits harmful outputs from safety-aligned models, with effectiveness varying by model.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The main attack results combine the AdvBench subset and HEx-PHI sample rather than reporting them separately. No uncertainty estimates are given. Bypass Rate uses a refusal keyword dictionary, and the paper notes this can misclassify off-topic or ethical-advice responses; harmfulness scoring is performed by GPT-4. Some baseline results are from prior papers rather than this study's own runs.
record.rows_left_out: Not included: defense-method results in Table 2, scene/purpose ablations in Figure 5 and Table 4, the Claude adaptation in Table 5, and the truthful-defense results in Table 6. These concern FFA variants or defenses rather than the first-token or suffix mechanism tested for V4.

untested.parts: No prefilling of a compliant opening, no decoding changes, and no analysis of whether GCG works by getting past the first response tokens.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No test of data or objective as the cause of shallowness.

missing.what: GCG result on Claude-3: BPR 2%, AHS 1.16, ASR 4%

record.verdict_notes: r1-r6 are baseline comparators for FFA, not the paper's focus, but they are the study's own measurements of an absolute suffix-attack rate, so they are kept as V4 rows. GCG values for GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Gemini carry a dagger (from prior papers) and are rightly excluded. Bypass rate uses a refusal keyword dictionary, and harmfulness is judged by GPT-4. Vicuna-7b is weakly safety-tuned, which may inflate the supporting result. AutoDAN, DeepInception and ArtPrompt are not opening-token mechanisms and do not bear on V4.

versions.untested_parts: Tests GCG's adversarial suffix attack, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes; does not test whether any of these work by getting past the first response tokens.
No weight or rank localization experiment.
No experiment on data or objective as the cause of shallow safety.
No training to deepen safety or test of whether deepened safety holds up.

relationships.condition: GCG suffix attack, Vicuna-7b, no defense
relationships.reason: Bypass rate rose from 4.4% to 96.3%, AHS from 1.09 to 4.09 and ASR from 0% to 66.2% (r1, r2, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Bypass rate rose from 4.4% to 96.3%, AHS from 1.09 to 4.09, and ASR from 0% to 66.2%.

relationships.condition: GCG suffix attack, LLaMA-3-8B, no defense
relationships.reason: Bypass rate was only 38.1%, AHS 1.96 and ASR 8.8%, much weaker than on Vicuna-7b (r4, r5, r6).
relationships.display_finding: On LLaMA-3-8B, GCG reached a bypass rate of 38.1%, an average harmfulness score of 1.96 and an attack success rate of 8.8%, much weaker than on Vicuna-7b.

relationships.condition: GCG suffix on Claude-3, Appendix Table 5 (presumably transferred)
relationships.reason: From the text, not the rows: GCG reached BPR 2%, AHS 1.16 and ASR 4% on Claude-3, so the suffix largely fails there. No row records this.
relationships.display_finding: On Claude-3, GCG reached a bypass rate of 2%, an average harmfulness score of 1.16 and an attack success rate of 4%, so the suffix largely failed.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: GCG produced a 96.3% bypass rate and a 66.2% attack success rate, supporting suffix-based bypass in this model (r1, r3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The bypass rate was 38.1%, while the attack success rate was 8.8%, showing a substantially weaker effect than on Vicuna-7b (r4, r5, r6).
